passage:
The eighteenth-century career of the sublime is often narrated as a tidy succession in which Edmund Burke's physiological account of terror yielded, after half a century, to Immanuel Kant's austerely cognitive one; Friedrich Schiller is then sometimes appended as a postscript who domesticated Kant's doctrine for a more recognizably moral audience. The narrative has the virtue of simplicity, but its simplicity flatters our habit of reading aesthetic history as a progression from body to mind. A closer look at the arguments themselves suggests that the three thinkers differ less over whether the sublime is bodily or cognitive than over what, in the moment of sublime apprehension, a subject has actually done.

For Burke, what the subject has done is to register, at some remove from genuine peril, the approach of an object too vast or too threatening to be possessed in perception; the tension of nerve and sinew that ensues is not incidental but constitutive, and any account that strips it away mistakes a sign for its cause. Kant's celebrated rewriting of this view appears, on first reading, to dismiss Burke's physiology outright. Yet Kant's own account turns on a parallel insufficiency, this time within the faculties themselves: imagination fails to render an overwhelming magnitude or force as a single intuition, and reason, registering that failure, seizes on it as evidence of its own supersensible vocation. The feeling of the sublime is the feeling of this two-step — defeat followed by discovery — and while it is not the tremor of a body in the presence of a threat, it is no less a report on a process the subject has undergone.

Schiller's contribution, often read as a watering-down, is in fact the most radical of the three. For Schiller the sublime is not primarily a response to an object at all but a rehearsal the subject undertakes against the conditions of its own finitude. The soul that has contemplated the storm at sea or the ruin of empires has practiced, in miniature, standing free of what would otherwise coerce it; the aesthetic feeling is prospective rather than retrospective, a preparation rather than a report. What looks like Kantian moralization is in fact a relocation of the sublime's center of gravity from event to exercise.

It would be a mistake, then, to read these three as successive refinements of a single doctrine. Each identifies a different site — the sentient body, the cognitive faculties, the ethical will in training — at which the sublime is said to occur. The question each is answering is not the same, even when the examples adduced (the storm, the mountain, the conflagration) happen to coincide. That the tradition has remembered them as a series owes more, perhaps, to the tidiness of textbooks than to the actual shape of their disagreement.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Although commonly arranged as successive refinements of one doctrine, Burke, Kant, and Schiller in fact locate the sublime in three different aspects of the subject's activity, and reading them as a sequence obscures this disagreement.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Kant's cognitive rewriting of Burke's physiological account of the sublime has been overstated; the two thinkers agree that the sublime is fundamentally a report on a process the subject has undergone.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Schiller's treatment of the sublime, far from being a watering-down of Kant's, is the most philosophically adventurous of the three eighteenth-century treatments and ought to displace the standard narrative.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The standard textbook narrative, in which Burke's physiological sublime yields to Kant's cognitive sublime and then to Schiller's moralized version, captures the shape of an intellectual progression from body to mind.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Because Burke, Kant, and Schiller draw on the same illustrative examples — storms, mountains, and conflagrations — their theories of the sublime cannot in the end be sharply distinguished from one another.

explanations.correct: The passage opens by criticizing the 'tidy succession' narrative and closes by saying the three thinkers identify different sites (sentient body, cognitive faculties, ethical will) and are not answering the same question. A captures both halves.
explanations.B: Picks up a nuance (the author does say Kant's account is not straightforwardly anti-Burkean) and inflates it into the thesis; the author does not claim the two agree on a shared process.
explanations.C: Paragraph-level restatement of the passage's remark about Schiller; the main point is about all three, not the elevation of one.
explanations.D: Endorses the narrative the passage explicitly criticizes as a flattery of our reading habits.
explanations.E: Reverses the author's position: shared examples are precisely what the passage says has misled readers into treating the three as answering the same question.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the received account of the eighteenth-century sublime can most accurately be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: outright repudiation of its central claims as historically false

choices.label: B
choices.text: skeptical of its tidiness but prepared to grant that it captures something genuine in the thinkers' examples

choices.label: C
choices.text: indifferent, since the author is concerned with the doctrines themselves rather than with how they have been narrated

choices.label: D
choices.text: enthusiasm for its treatment of Kant offset by reservations about its treatment of Schiller

choices.label: E
choices.text: admiration for its pedagogical economy but rejection of the progressivist metaphysics it implies

explanations.correct: The author calls the narrative tidy and traces its appeal to textbook convenience, yet concedes that the thinkers' illustrative examples 'happen to coincide' and never denies that the account captures a pattern; this is skepticism that stops short of repudiation.
explanations.A: Too strong — the author says the received account has the virtue of simplicity and criticizes only what that simplicity obscures.
explanations.C: The passage is explicitly evaluative of the received narrative, not indifferent.
explanations.D: The author criticizes the received treatment of both Kant (dismissing Burke outright) and Schiller (as a mere postscript); splitting the critique by figure misreads it.
explanations.E: Overstates the author's endorsement — 'admiration for its pedagogical economy' is not in the passage, and the critique is not merely of metaphysics.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A standard narrative is described; its appeal is acknowledged; three positions are examined in turn to show where they actually differ; the narrative's persistence is explained by a consideration other than fidelity to the arguments.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A dispute among three thinkers is introduced; each thinker's position is summarized in neutral terms; a fourth position is offered as a synthesis; objections to the synthesis are canvassed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A claim is defended chronologically from its earliest statement to its most recent; objections raised at each stage are rebutted before the narrative advances.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Three aesthetic positions are contrasted with a fourth, unnamed position held by the author; the author's position is then shown to reconcile the earlier three.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A historical puzzle is posed; two candidate solutions are weighed against each other; the second is endorsed; its implications for a related tradition are drawn out.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 presents the standard narrative and its appeal; paragraphs 2-3 walk through Burke, Kant, and Schiller to relocate each; paragraph 4 explains the narrative's persistence by appeal to textbook tidiness. A tracks this exactly.
explanations.B: No fourth synthesizing position appears; the author's move is to separate the three, not to synthesize them.
explanations.C: The passage is anti-progressivist; it does not defend a single claim across stages or canvass stage-by-stage rebuttals.
explanations.D: No unnamed fourth position is introduced, and the author does not reconcile the three.
explanations.E: There is no contest between two candidate solutions; the author rejects one narrative without offering a rival historical solution of that form.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would be likely to assent to which one of the following claims?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A theorist who sought to combine Burke's physiological account with Schiller's ethical account would be attempting to reconcile positions that answer different questions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because imagination plays a central role in Kant's account, Kant should be read as having accepted, at a deeper level, Burke's claim that the sublime is fundamentally a bodily phenomenon.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Schiller's treatment of the sublime loses plausibility to the extent that the subject's preparatory exercise takes place in the absence of any actual storm or ruin.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A satisfactory theory of the sublime must identify, within the subject, a single faculty whose activity is common to all cases in which the sublime is felt.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Burke's insistence on the constitutive role of tension of nerve and sinew is the weakest element of his theory and is better dropped.

explanations.correct: The author insists each of the three locates the sublime in a different 'site' and that they are not answering the same question. A theorist attempting to combine two such accounts would therefore be trying to reconcile answers to distinct questions — exactly what the author says has long been obscured.
explanations.B: Reverses the author's point: Kant's imagination-failure is a 'parallel insufficiency' within the faculties, not a concealed endorsement of Burke's bodily view.
explanations.C: Schiller's whole point, as the author presents it, is that the sublime for Schiller is not primarily a response to an object; the author would not treat the absence of the object as diminishing its plausibility.
explanations.D: The passage's organizing claim is that the three theorists locate the sublime at different sites; the author gives no sign of demanding a single faculty across cases.
explanations.E: The author is explicitly sympathetic to Burke's point that the physiological element is constitutive rather than incidental.

questions.questionStem: The author's remark that Schiller's contribution is 'often read as a watering-down' (third paragraph) functions in the passage primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: concede a point to readers who would deny that Schiller belongs in a discussion of the sublime at all

choices.label: B
choices.text: introduce a received impression of Schiller that the author then overturns in order to show how radically Schiller relocates the sublime

choices.label: C
choices.text: identify the chief weakness of Schiller's account and explain why Kant's treatment is to be preferred

choices.label: D
choices.text: illustrate the 'progression from body to mind' that the author endorses as the best way of organizing the tradition

choices.label: E
choices.text: contrast Schiller's approach with Burke's in order to argue that Schiller recovers what Kant had abandoned

explanations.correct: The clause is set up in order to be reversed: the author says Schiller is 'in fact the most radical of the three,' and the sentence then explains why. Its function is to introduce a received view the author rebuts.
explanations.A: No such denial is at issue; the author treats Schiller's membership in the tradition as given.
explanations.C: The author does not prefer Kant to Schiller; he argues that the two are not even answering the same question.
explanations.D: The 'progression from body to mind' is described as the flattering habit the author criticizes, not as his own organizing principle.
explanations.E: The sentence makes no contrast with Burke and advances no recovery claim; the contrast in the sentence is between the received reading of Schiller and the author's.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following scenarios most closely illustrates the account of the sublime that the passage attributes to Schiller?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A hiker trembles at the sight of an approaching thunderstorm and afterward records the physiological sensations that the storm produced.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A philosopher, confronted with the night sky, notes that imagination fails to represent its extent and infers from this failure the supersensible scope of reason.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A novice climber deliberately contemplates the ruin of an ancient fortress in order to strengthen, against future adversity, her capacity to remain unshaken by loss.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A historian catalogues the conflagrations of several cities and argues that their similarity shows a single underlying aesthetic principle at work.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A painter selects a mountain scene for its visual drama and paints it in a way designed to produce in the viewer a nervous apprehension of scale.

explanations.correct: Schiller's sublime, on the passage's reading, is a prospective rehearsal against finitude — the subject practices standing free of what would otherwise coerce her. The climber contemplating the ruin in order to strengthen herself against future adversity matches that mechanism exactly.
explanations.A: Reports a physiological response after the fact — this is Burke's account, not Schiller's.
explanations.B: Tracks Kant's two-step of imagination-failure and reason's self-discovery, not Schiller's prospective exercise.
explanations.D: Describes a historian's empirical comparison rather than an exercise undertaken by the subject against her own finitude.
explanations.E: Focuses on producing an apprehension in a viewer — again closer to Burke's physiological framing than to Schiller's preparatory exercise.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most undermine the author's claim that Burke, Kant, and Schiller are not answering the same question?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Schiller's lectures, now lost, reportedly acknowledged Burke's physiological description as a special case of a more general account that Schiller himself developed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Kant's correspondence with colleagues shows that he was aware of Burke's treatise in its German translation and approved of its examples.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A close comparison of the three theorists' definitions reveals that each, despite differences in vocabulary, defines the sublime as a specific modification of a single faculty of the subject and addresses the identical question of what that modification is.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Eighteenth-century readers typically encountered the three texts in the order in which they were written, and commentators of the period already treated them as a developmental sequence.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The examples of storms, mountains, and conflagrations that appear in all three accounts were drawn from a shared stock of illustrations circulated in contemporary rhetorical handbooks.

explanations.correct: The author's claim is that each theorist locates the sublime at a distinct site and that the question each is answering is not the same. A demonstration that all three in fact define the sublime as a modification of a single faculty and are addressing the identical question would undermine that claim directly.
explanations.A: A concession by Schiller that Burke's account is a special case of his own would support, not undermine, the author's picture of divergent questions subsuming Burke under Schiller.
explanations.B: Kant's awareness of and approval of Burke's examples is consistent with the author's view that the shared examples have misled readers about the shape of the disagreement.
explanations.D: The author already acknowledges that the tradition has remembered the three as a series; contemporary commentators doing the same is not new evidence against his diagnosis.
explanations.E: Provides a further explanation of why the examples overlap — consistent with, not a threat to, the author's position that shared examples mask differing questions.

passage:
To speak of the structuralist revolution in literary study is already to concede a framing that the movement's most careful practitioners would have resisted. Roland Barthes, in his earlier phase, is sometimes enrolled as the movement's great popularizer; Tzvetan Todorov, as its taxonomist of narrative forms; Gérard Genette, as its most austere theorist of narrative discourse. Each was, at one time or another, willing to describe his project as the extension to literature of the method Ferdinand de Saussure had proposed for language. Yet to arrange these three in a single column under the heading "structuralism" is to understate the differences in what each thought such an extension would require, and in what each believed it could deliver.

Todorov's early grammars of narrative sought what he called the "poetics" of the literary text — not a reading of any particular work but a specification of the underlying system of possibilities from which particular works are drawn. He pursued this with a confidence, later muted, that the system could in principle be fully described, and that any sufficiently careful reader could recover it from the works themselves. Genette's undertaking was more guarded. His categories of order, duration, and frequency were designed to register what a narrative does, but he treated his own apparatus as a descriptive instrument rather than as a discovery about narrative in general, and he repeatedly warned against confusing the map he was drawing with a territory that could exist independently of it. Barthes, by contrast, had by the late 1960s grown suspicious of the very project of a general poetics; his celebrated argument that the text is a "tissue of quotations" rather than the expression of a single intending author pushed against the structuralist confidence that literary works could be referred to an underlying system at all.

It is tempting to read Barthes's later turn as simply anti-structuralist and therefore as a repudiation of Todorov and Genette alike. The temptation should be resisted. Barthes continued to hold — and this is easy to miss — that literary works participate in codes, conventions, and shared stocks of meaning; his quarrel was not with the thought that such codes are at work, but with the thought that a critic's listing of them exhausts what criticism can say. Todorov's and Genette's projects, on his mature view, were not wrong so much as terminal: they described one layer of the text and then stopped where the harder work begins.

Seen this way, the standard narrative — structuralism rises with Todorov, is refined by Genette, and is dismantled by Barthes — captures the chronology but misrepresents the disagreement. All three accepted that literature operates through codes; they parted over whether recovering the codes constitutes the critic's work, supplements it, or ends only where the critic's work properly begins.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The standard narrative that structuralism rose with Todorov, was refined by Genette, and was dismantled by Barthes is chronologically accurate, and its account of the theoretical relations among the three is broadly correct as well.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Barthes's later work, properly understood, marks a full repudiation of the structuralist projects of Todorov and Genette, whose methods Barthes's argument for the text as a tissue of quotations makes obsolete.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Although Todorov, Genette, and Barthes are often grouped together as structuralists who broke in stages from a common project, their disagreement is better understood as concerning the status of the critic's work with respect to the codes that organize literary texts.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Genette's cautious treatment of his descriptive apparatus as a map rather than a territory represents the most defensible version of the structuralist program and ought to displace the more ambitious account pursued by Todorov.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The extension of Saussure's linguistic method to literature, undertaken in different ways by Todorov, Genette, and Barthes, ultimately failed because the structuralist assumption of an underlying system of literary possibilities cannot be sustained.

explanations.correct: The passage opens by resisting a uniform 'structuralism' label, contrasts the three thinkers' positions on whether the critic's work is constituted by, supplements, or only begins after the recovery of codes, and closes by saying the standard narrative misrepresents the disagreement. C integrates all three strands.
explanations.A: The passage explicitly says the standard narrative misrepresents the disagreement, even while granting the chronology.
explanations.B: The passage warns explicitly against reading Barthes's later turn as a simple repudiation of Todorov and Genette.
explanations.D: Paragraph-level restatement: the passage treats Genette's caution sympathetically but does not argue he should displace Todorov.
explanations.E: Too strong — the author never claims structuralism 'failed,' and all three thinkers are credited with identifying something real about codes in literary texts.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the mature Barthes would object to which one of the following descriptions of a critic's work?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A critic who, having identified the generic conventions that a poem draws upon, proceeds to examine what the poem achieves by drawing upon them in just the way it does.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A critic who catalogues the narrative codes operative in a short story and, having catalogued them, presents the catalogue as a complete account of the story.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A critic who, while acknowledging that literary codes are at work in a novel, focuses her essay on the tensions and silences that the codes alone cannot explain.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A critic who denies that literary works can be referred to any underlying code or convention whatsoever, treating each work as wholly sui generis.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A critic who treats a descriptive apparatus as a map drawn for particular analytic purposes rather than as a territory existing independently of the critic's concerns.

explanations.correct: Barthes's mature view, according to the passage, accepts that codes are at work but denies that listing them exhausts what criticism can say. A critic who presents the catalogue of codes as a complete account does exactly what Barthes says one should not do.
explanations.A: Describes precisely the further work Barthes thinks begins where code-listing ends; he would endorse it.
explanations.C: Describes the kind of critical attention Barthes on the passage's account would endorse — not object to.
explanations.D: The passage explicitly says Barthes continued to hold that codes and conventions are at work; he would also reject this description.
explanations.E: Matches Genette's stance, which Barthes treats as 'not wrong' but incomplete; the object of Barthes's objection is completing with such a description, not adopting one.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward Todorov's early work can most accurately be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: unreserved admiration for the ambition of its systematizing project

choices.label: B
choices.text: respect for the project, accompanied by recognition that the confidence that animated it was later tempered even by Todorov himself

choices.label: C
choices.text: sharp disapproval of its commitment to a general poetics and endorsement of Genette's more guarded alternative in its place

choices.label: D
choices.text: indifference, since the author's primary interest lies in Barthes's later repudiation of structuralist method

choices.label: E
choices.text: enthusiasm for its descriptive economy, offset by reservations about its dependence on Saussure

explanations.correct: The passage describes Todorov's project in substantive terms without pejorative language and notes explicitly that his confidence was 'later muted.' The author neither dismisses the project nor endorses it without qualification.
explanations.A: Overstated positivity; 'later muted' signals that the author recognizes the confidence was not sustained.
explanations.C: The author does not express disapproval of Todorov's general-poetics commitment and does not elevate Genette above him.
explanations.D: The passage devotes a substantial portion of paragraph 2 to Todorov and treats his project as central to the disagreement; it is not indifferent.
explanations.E: 'Reservations about its dependence on Saussure' is not in the passage; the author does not critique the Saussurean lineage as such.

questions.questionStem: The author's description of Genette's apparatus as a 'map' rather than a 'territory' (second paragraph) serves primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: contrast Genette's methodological caution with Todorov's more confident assumption that a system of narrative possibilities awaits discovery in the works themselves

choices.label: B
choices.text: align Genette's position with Barthes's later skepticism about any attempt to refer literary works to an underlying system

choices.label: C
choices.text: illustrate the extension of Saussurean method to literature by invoking a cartographic metaphor drawn from linguistics

choices.label: D
choices.text: argue that Genette's categories of order, duration, and frequency are too provisional to count as a contribution to narrative theory

choices.label: E
choices.text: anticipate Barthes's argument that the text is a tissue of quotations and that no author's intention underlies it

explanations.correct: Immediately before the map/territory remark, the passage says Todorov thought the system could in principle be fully described and recovered from the works; the map/territory distinction is deployed to mark the contrast with Genette's more guarded, instrument-not-discovery stance.
explanations.B: The passage treats Genette and Barthes as distinct — Barthes's objection runs deeper than methodological caution about an apparatus. The map/territory language belongs to Genette, not to a shared skepticism.
explanations.C: The cartographic metaphor is not invoked as an illustration of Saussurean method; it is invoked to distinguish two attitudes toward one's own theoretical apparatus.
explanations.D: The author presents Genette's caution as principled, not as evidence that his categories are too provisional to be a contribution.
explanations.E: Barthes's later argument is about quotation and authorship, not about the status of a descriptive apparatus as map versus territory.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, each of the following is true of the mature Barthes EXCEPT:

choices.label: A
choices.text: He grew suspicious of the project of a general poetics of the literary text.

choices.label: B
choices.text: He continued to hold that literary works participate in codes, conventions, and shared stocks of meaning.

choices.label: C
choices.text: He regarded Todorov's and Genette's projects as terminal rather than as simply mistaken.

choices.label: D
choices.text: He argued that the text is a tissue of quotations rather than the expression of a single intending author.

choices.label: E
choices.text: He maintained that recovering the codes at work in a literary text is, by itself, the central task of literary criticism.

explanations.correct: The passage specifically says Barthes's quarrel was with the thought that a critic's listing of codes 'exhausts what criticism can say' — the opposite of maintaining that recovering them is the critic's central task. All other choices are directly stated.
explanations.A: Stated in paragraph 2 ('grown suspicious of the very project of a general poetics').
explanations.B: Stated in paragraph 3 ('Barthes continued to hold ... that literary works participate in codes, conventions, and shared stocks of meaning').
explanations.C: Stated in paragraph 3 ('not wrong so much as terminal').
explanations.D: Stated in paragraph 2 ('the text is a tissue of quotations rather than the expression of a single intending author').
explanations.E: Correct — this is the position the passage says Barthes rejects.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following critical practices most closely conforms to the conception of criticism that the passage attributes to the mature Barthes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A scholar identifies the conventions of pastoral poetry at work in a seventeenth-century elegy and rests her reading on that identification.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A scholar denies that any genre conventions inform a contemporary novel and reads the novel strictly as the expression of its author's personal voice.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A scholar, having identified the generic codes a short story relies upon, devotes the bulk of her essay to what the story does with those codes and to the tensions they leave unresolved.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A scholar constructs a taxonomy of plot types in the realist novel and argues that individual novels are fully characterized once their place in the taxonomy is located.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A scholar argues that a poem's meaning is exhausted by a careful reconstruction of its author's biographical intentions at the time of composition.

explanations.correct: The mature Barthes on the passage's account accepts that codes are at work but insists the harder critical work begins where the cataloguing of codes ends. The scholar who identifies the codes and then focuses on what the story does with them and on the tensions they leave unresolved exemplifies that conception.
explanations.A: Mirrors the 'terminal' practice Barthes treated as stopping short of the harder work.
explanations.B: Denies the operation of conventions altogether — contrary to Barthes's continuing commitment to codes.
explanations.D: Matches Todorov's early confidence that individual works are fully recovered by their place in a system, the very stance Barthes's later position resists.
explanations.E: Returns to the author-intention model that Barthes's tissue-of-quotations argument explicitly targets.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most support the author's contention that Barthes's later turn should not be read as a simple repudiation of Todorov and Genette?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Barthes, in unpublished lectures from his later career, described Todorov's poetics and Genette's narratology as indispensable preliminaries to the kind of reading he himself sought to practice.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Todorov, in essays published shortly after Barthes's death, conceded that the general poetics he had once pursued could not in principle be completed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Genette responded to Barthes's tissue-of-quotations argument by withdrawing his own categories of order, duration, and frequency from later editions of his work.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several early readers of Barthes's later essays took them to recommend abandoning any reference to codes and conventions in the reading of literary texts.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Saussure's original linguistic writings had already been used, long before Barthes, to motivate repudiations of structuralist approaches to literature.

explanations.correct: The author's specific contention is that Barthes's mature view treats Todorov's and Genette's work as 'not wrong so much as terminal.' Evidence that Barthes himself described their projects as indispensable preliminaries to his own reading directly supports that non-repudiation reading.
explanations.B: A concession by Todorov about the limits of his own early project is about Todorov, not about Barthes's relation to him; it leaves untouched whether Barthes repudiated or only supplemented him.
explanations.C: If Genette had withdrawn his categories in response to Barthes, that would tend to support the repudiation reading the author resists — the wrong direction.
explanations.D: Early readers taking Barthes to recommend abandonment of codes is evidence for the repudiation reading the author wants to block, not against it.
explanations.E: A pre-Barthesian use of Saussure to attack structuralist literary method tells us nothing about Barthes's own stance toward Todorov and Genette.
